chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Abu Ayoub, from Muhammad ibn Muslim, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family), at the beginning of his mission, would fast continuously until it was said, 'He will not break his fast,' and he would break his fast continuously until it was said, 'He will not fast.' Then he abandoned that and fasted one day and broke fast one day, which is the fast of David (peace be upon him). Then he abandoned that and fasted the three white days (13th, 14th, 15th). Then he abandoned that and distributed it, fasting two days in every ten days, with a Wednesday in between two Thursdays. So he was taken (died), and peace be upon him and his family, while he was still acting upon that.

key_terms.الْأَيَّامِ الْغُرِّ: The white days, referring to the 13th, 14th, and 15th of the lunar month
key_terms.صَوْمُ دَاوُدَ: The fast of David, referring to fasting one day and breaking fast the next
key_terms.وَالْآلِ السَّلَامُ: And the family (peace be upon them)
key_terms.يَوْمَا خَمِيسَيْنِ: Two Thursdays, indicating a specific pattern of fasting days within a ten-day cycle

ai.seo_question: What was the chronological progression of the Prophet's fasting habits before the final ruling was established?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi outlines the historical evolution of the Prophet Muhammad’s (SAWW) voluntary fasting, tracing a progression from continuous abstinence to the balanced practice of Sawm Dawud, and finally to a fixed rhythm of fasting two days in every ten. This final pattern, which he maintained until his death, serves as a key scholarly reference for understanding the Sunnah of regular, moderate voluntary fasting (Sawm al-Tatawwu') in Shia tradition, emphasizing consistency over intensity.
